name: Cervical pillow

lead: A cervical pillow has a contoured curve or raised roll that supports the natural curve of the neck while you sleep. People use it for better neck alignment and comfortable sleep, and in appearance circles for less morning stiffness and puffiness from sleep position.

The contour aims to keep the neck closer to neutral and spread pressure. A 2021 meta-analysis of pillow trials found spring and rubber pillows reduced neck pain, waking symptoms and disability in chronic neck pain, and that shape and height influenced alignment more than filling. Studies mostly look at neck pain and sleep comfort; facial appearance has not been tested.

paras: People swap it in for their regular pillow, in memory foam, latex or spring designs, and sleep on their back or side. Fit varies by sleep position and body build, so many try more than one shape.
A pillow that suits one sleeper can cause discomfort for another. Trials are small and of mixed quality, and no study has shown it changes daytime posture or facial appearance.

angle.text: Supporting the neck during sleep aims for less strain, better sleep and a more neutral position, which users link to less morning stiffness and puffiness. Trials look at neck pain and sleep comfort; the facial effects are user-reported.

lead: A cervical pillow is a contoured or roll-shaped pillow designed to support the natural curve of the neck during sleep. Designs include a raised ridge under the neck with a shallower hollow for the head, cylindrical rolls, and adjustable or semi-customized shapes, and materials range from memory foam and latex to spring and fibre fillings. [1][2]

Manufacturers market them for neck comfort and spinal alignment, and they are also discussed in appearance and posture circles as a possible aid for morning neck stiffness. Clinicians have studied cervical pillows mainly in people with chronic neck pain, in sleep-disordered breathing and as a positioning aid during eye surgery, rather than for appearance outcomes. [3][4][5][6]

Published evidence is modest. A 2021 systematic review and meta-analysis of pillow design examined effects on neck pain, waking symptoms, disability, sleep quality and spinal alignment, and small trials of specific contoured pillows have reported reduced neck pain compared with participants' own pillows. Trials are generally small and of mixed quality, and no published study has tested whether a cervical pillow changes daytime posture or facial appearance. [7][8][9]
infobox: Chronic neck pain, sleep-disordered breathing, surgical positioning
Consumer product; some designs sold as orthopedic aids

paras: Pillows in general are older than recorded history in the form of rigid headrests, and soft stuffed pillows developed later in several regions, according to a general reference article on pillows. [1] A cervical pillow is a modern specialisation of the form, shaped to fill the gap between the head and the mattress under the neck. [2]

Common designs include a wave or butterfly profile with a higher neck ridge and a lower central cradle, and a firm cylindrical roll placed beneath the neck. Some trial pillows were custom-fitted or semi-customized to the user's measurements rather than mass-produced. [10][11][12]

sections.h: How it is intended to work
paras: The design aim is to keep the cervical spine closer to a neutral alignment while lying down and to spread pressure across the head and neck. A 2021 review of pillow trials concluded that the shape and height of a pillow influenced alignment more than its filling. [7]

Pillow performance also interacts with the mattress. An experimental and finite-element study using a cervical pillow on soft, medium and hard mattresses reported that on a soft mattress the head and cervical lordosis distances increased and modelled intervertebral disc loading rose by about 49 percent compared with a medium mattress, and the authors suggested that a softer or thinner pillow may suit a soft mattress. [13]
No study has examined cervical pillows for posture correction or facial appearance. The research that exists addresses pain, sleep and clinical positioning.
A 2021 systematic review and meta-analysis in Clinical Biomechanics evaluated pillow design effects on neck pain, waking symptoms, neck disability, sleep quality and spinal alignment. [7]

A 1998 before-and-after study of 28 people with chronic neck pain tested a roll-shaped cylindrical pillow and measured pain severity and use of headache or neck-pain medication. [11] A 2004 randomized trial of 36 adults with chronic biomechanical neck pain, with or without headache, tested a semi-customized experimental cervical pillow over four weeks. [10]

A 2017 preliminary comparative study of 12 recreational athletes with chronic mechanical neck pain reported that scores for pain and disability, tympanic temperature and a heart-rate-variability ratio were significantly lower after using the experimental pillow than after using their own pillows, and that 80 percent of participants rated it perfectly comfortable. The study was small, had no randomized control group and tested one specific design. [8]

A trial protocol published in 2025 describes a participant-blinded, three-arm pilot randomized trial of different pillows in people with cervical spondylosis, measuring sleep quality and disability; the protocol reports no results. [9]

A 1983 study radiographically evaluated cervical curve depth in 35 patients with loss of the normal curve who received chiropractic manipulation, with one subgroup also given an orthopedic cervical pillow for home use. The comparison groups were very small. [14]

Two studies from a sleep clinic tested a custom-fitted pillow that promoted head extension in people with obstructive sleep apnea. In a 1999 trial of 12 participants, people with mild disease showed a significant improvement in the respiratory disturbance index, those with moderate disease showed no improvement, and those with severe disease showed slight improvement on some measures. [3] A 2001 study of 18 people with mild-to-moderate disease reported a significant trend toward improved respiratory disturbance index and fewer arousals. Both studies were small and used a specialised design not equivalent to retail cervical pillows. [5]

A 2024 randomized controlled trial of 104 patients undergoing cataract surgery compared supine positioning with and without a cervical pillow. The pillow group reported lower discomfort and higher patient and surgeon satisfaction, with no significant difference in head displacement. [4]

No serious adverse effects are prominent in the trial literature. Studies and manufacturers both note that comfort is individual; the 2021 review and trials focus on specific pillow designs rather than a single standard shape, and findings in one design do not necessarily carry over to another. [7][8]
Because the mattress and sleep position affect how a pillow sits, the mattress study suggests that the same pillow can produce different neck alignment on different surfaces. [13]

In appearance-oriented communities, cervical pillows are sometimes mentioned alongside posture tools as a low-cost aid for neck position at night. No published research supports effects on daytime posture, forward-head posture or facial appearance from a sleep pillow. [7]

timeline.event: A short article titled "The cervical pillow" appears in the Journal of the Indian Medical Association. [6]
A small study examines an orthopedic cervical pillow alongside chiropractic care for loss of cervical curve. [14]
A before-and-after study tests a cylindrical cervical pillow in chronic neck pain. [11]
A sleep-clinic study tests a custom cervical pillow in obstructive sleep apnea. [3]
A randomized trial tests a semi-customized cervical pillow in chronic neck pain with and without headache. [10]
A systematic review and meta-analysis of pillow design is published in Clinical Biomechanics. [7]
